[start-outcomes] After this part you should be able to
1. Apply Galerkin and integration by parts to the plane-stress PDE, identify [k], {q} and {b}, and write [B] = [∂]ᵀ[N] and [k] = t∫[B]ᵀ[E][B] dA.
2. Evaluate the 8 × 8 stiffness matrix of a four-node rectangular element from the closed-form entries s_1 …s_{12} , and check it.
3. Convert edge tractions and body forces into equivalent nodal loads, assemble the global system with two dofs per node and impose displacement conditions.
4. Solve the 2 × 2 cantilever, check its reactions, compare it with beam theory and a refined mesh, and explain why the coarse mesh is too stiff.

[notes-n1] Notes 1. Galerkin and integration by parts, two unknowns per node
Plane Stress Part 1 ended with two results: the PDE [∂][E][∂]ᵀ{u}ᵀ = −{f} and the interpolation {u}ᵀ = [N]{û}ᵀ with the 2 × 8 matrix [N]. Substitute the second into the first and, as in Heat Transfer Part 2, it does not balance: a bilinear displacement field cannot satisfy two second-order equations at every point.
EQUATION (3.31): [equation r_subst: source not available in the page]
Galerkin, vector version Weight the residual with [N]ᵀ, the transpose of the interpolation matrix, and ask that each weighted average be zero. [N]ᵀ is 8 × 2, so one element gives eight equations, one per degree of freedom: u_1, v_1, …, u_4, v_4.
EQUATION (3.32): [equation r_weighted: source not available in the page]
## Integration by parts, then name the terms
Exactly as for heat, one [∂] moves from the displacements onto the weight [N]ᵀ (Green’s theorem, applied to each row). The derivative order falls to one, so a bilinear field is admissible, and a boundary integral appears that carries the traction, the natural condition of Plane Stress Part 1.
EQUATION (3.34)–(3.38): [equation r_rearr: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (3.38): [equation r_sys: source not available in the page]
Term Name What it holds Heat analogue
[k] stiffness matrix material, geometry and thickness of the element; symmetric; 8 × 8 conductance matrix, 4 × 4
{q} body-force vector forces per unit volume inside the element (self-weight), shared among its nodes source vector
{b} traction vector forces on edges with a known traction; zero on free edges; discarded with the equation on fixed edges boundary-flux vector
Which edges of the cantilever contribute to {b}? Only the free end, x = 4 m, with its downward traction. The top and bottom edges are free (b_x = b_y = 0), so their boundary term vanishes. On the fixed edge the traction is unknown, but it multiplies the shape functions of nodes whose equations are struck when u = v = 0 is imposed; it comes back afterwards as the support reactions, just as the heat flow did at a prescribed temperature.
Key points:
- Weight the residual with [N]ᵀ: eight equations per four-node element.
- Integration by parts lowers the derivative order and exposes the traction as the natural condition.
- [k]{û}ᵀ = {q} + {b} = {r}: stiffness, body force, traction; the same structure as heat with two unknowns per node.
Quick check (not graded): Weighting the plane-stress residual with [N]ᵀ gives, for one four-node element,
Options: four equations, one per node | eight equations, one per degree of freedom | two equations, one per direction
Explanation shown after answering: [N]ᵀ is 8 × 2 and the residual is 2 × 1, so the weighted residual is an 8 × 1 vector: one equation for each of u_1, v_1, …, u_4, v_4. Heat transfer gave four, one per node, because it had one unknown per node.

[notes-n2] Notes 2. The strain–displacement matrix [B] and the stiffness matrix
In heat transfer the 2 × 4 matrix {∂}ᵀ{N} turned the nodal temperatures into the gradient. Its plane-stress counterpart turns the eight nodal displacements into the three strains, and it has a name of its own: the strain–displacement matrix [B].
EQUATION : [equation r_B_def: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation r_B: source not available in the page]
- Row 1 (ε_{xx} = ∂u/∂x): ∂N_i/∂x under each u_i, zero under each v_i.
- Row 2 (ε_{yy} = ∂v/∂y): ∂N_i/∂y under each v_i, zero under each u_i.
- Row 3 (ε_{xy} = ∂u/∂y + ∂v/∂x, the engineering shear strain): ∂N_i/∂y under u_i and ∂N_i/∂x under v_i.
Nothing new is computed Every entry of [B] is a shape-function derivative from Heat Transfer Part 1: ∂N_1/∂x = −(b − y)/(ab) = (y − b)/(ab), and so on. [B] only arranges them so that u and v are differentiated together.
## Worked step · [B] at (1.5, 0.3) of a 2 m × 1 m element (Activity 1)
The derivatives are those of the Heat Transfer Part 1 point: ∂N_i/∂x = {−0.35, 0.35, 0.15, −0.15} and ∂N_i/∂y = {−0.25, −0.75, 0.75, 0.25} m^{−1}. Place them in the three rows:
EQUATION : [equation v0_Bnum: source not available in the page]
Each row adds up to zero, and in row 3 the u-entries and the v-entries add up to zero separately. The reason is physical: a rigid translation (all u_i equal, all v_i equal) produces no strain. Keep this [B]; Plane Stress Part 3 multiplies it by the nodal displacements to get the stresses.
## The element stiffness matrix in [B] form
Integration by parts left the product [N]ᵀ[∂] on the left and [∂]ᵀ[N] on the right of [E]. Both are [B] (the left one transposed), so the stiffness matrix is the same [B] twice with the material between:
EQUATION : [equation r_kB: source not available in the page]
- Thickness. The integrals are per unit thickness; the element has thickness t, so every entry of [k] and every load is multiplied by t.
- Symmetry. [B]ᵀ[E][B] is symmetric whenever [E] is, and integration keeps it so: at most 36 distinct entries, and for a rectangle only twelve (§3).
- Meaning. k_{ij} is the force at dof i needed to give dof j a unit displacement with every other dof held: the stiffness influence coefficient of structural analysis.
## How software integrates [k]
[Figure: Software evaluates t[B]ᵀ[E][B] × det J at four Gauss points, ξ, η = ±1/√3, and adds them. For a rectangle the integrand is quadratic in each direction and the four-point sum equals the closed form of §3 exactly; for a distorted element like this one numerical integration is the only route. Image: PyMAPDL documentation, “Build a finite element model”, © ANSYS, Inc., MIT licence.]
Key points:
- [B] = [∂]ᵀ[N], 3 × 8: strains from nodal displacements; every row adds up to zero.
- [k] = t∫[B]ᵀ[E][B] dA, 8 × 8, symmetric; k_{ij} = force at i per unit displacement at j.
- Software integrates at 2 × 2 Gauss points; for a rectangle that is exact.
Quick check (not graded): Why must every row of [B] add up to zero?
Options: Because [B] is symmetric | Because each shape function is 1 at its own node | A rigid translation of the element produces no strain
Explanation shown after answering: Giving every node the same u (or the same v) moves the element without deforming it, so [B]{û}ᵀ must be zero; that is a sum of the u-entries (or the v-entries) of each row. [B] is 3 × 8 and cannot be symmetric; the Kronecker property is true but is not the reason.

[notes-n3] Notes 3. The 8 × 8 stiffness matrix and its twelve values
One entry in full is enough to see how all of them are made. Take k_{34}: row 3 belongs to u_2 and column 4 to v_2, so it couples the horizontal and the vertical displacement of the same node.
## k₃₄ in three steps (text (3.39)–(3.41))
EQUATION (3.39): [equation r_s1: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (3.40): [equation r_s2: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (3.41): [equation r_s3: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation r_s3b: source not available in the page]
The integral of −x(b − y)/(a²b²) over the rectangle is −1/4, so k_{34} does not depend on a or b: the coupling between u and v at a node is the same for every rectangle. The text writes the result as Et/(8(ν − 1)).
## Twelve values, one pattern
Repeating the integration for the other entries gives only twelve distinct values, arranged by the symmetry of the rectangle. Rows 1, 3, 5, 7 belong to u_1…u_4 and rows 2, 4, 6, 8 to v_1…v_4; k_{34} is s_6. You do not memorise the pattern: you read it correctly from the text.
EQUATION (3.42): [equation r_kfull: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation r_svals_a: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation r_svals_b: source not available in the page]
How to read the twelve values s_1, s_3, s_5, s_7 couple u with u: they are the heat conductance values with k_x = Et/(1 − ν²) and k_y = Gt (stretching along x, shearing along y). s_9…s_{12} couple v with v, the same with a and b swapped. s_2, s_4, s_6, s_8 couple u with v and contain no a or b.

All four elements of the 2 × 2 mesh have the same a, b and material, so this one matrix serves the whole mesh. The entries ±0.003 (s_4, s_8) are small because 1 − 3ν = 0.01 for ν = 0.33.
Checks on any [k] you compute Symmetric. In every row the u-entries add up to zero and so do the v-entries: a rigid translation in x or in y needs no force. A rigid rotation also gives [k]{d} = {0}. These three zero-energy modes make [k], and an unsupported [K], singular until the supports prevent them.
EQUATION : [equation r_rowsum: source not available in the page]
The usual traps Plane strain [E] used where plane stress is asked (or the reverse); a and b swapped between s_1 and s_9; a sign lost in s_4 = −s_8 or s_6 = −s_2. The row-sum check catches only the lost sign: the other two give a matrix that is wrong but still balanced, so settle Ē = E/(1 − ν²) and which side is a before computing anything.
Key points:
- Twelve values s_1…s_{12} in the pattern (3.42); the u–v couplings do not depend on a or b.
- Cantilever element: k_{11} = s_1 = 0.875 × 10⁶, s_2 = 0.373 × 10⁶, s_9 = 1.622 × 10⁶ N m^{−1}.
- u-entries and v-entries of every row sum to zero; three zero-energy modes.
Quick check (not graded): For ν = 1/3, the entries s_4 and s_8 of a rectangle are
Options: zero | equal to s_2 | the largest entries of [k]
Explanation shown after answering: s_8 = −s_4 = Et(1 − 3ν)/(8(1 − ν²)), and 1 − 3ν = 0 at ν = 1/3. That is why the cantilever element (ν = 0.33) shows only ±0.003 × 10⁶ there.

[notes-n4] Notes 4. Loads: edge tractions and body forces
The load vector follows the same rule as in heat transfer, now in the plane-stress dof order: along an edge only the shape functions of its two nodes are non-zero, and along that edge they are the linear functions of a bar. A uniform load is therefore shared equally by the two nodes, in the direction it acts and nowhere else.
[Figure: A uniform downward traction on edge 2–3 loads v_2 and v_3 equally.]
EQUATION : [equation r_bedge: source not available in the page]
EQUATION (3.45): [equation r_r2: source not available in the page]
Per length or per area? The text gives q_y = −5 kN m^{−1}: a load per unit length of edge for the whole thickness. A traction in kN m^{−2} must be multiplied by t first. In (3.45) the t of the integral cancels the 1/t of q_y/t, which is why the thickness disappears from the result.
## A linearly varying edge load
If the load per unit length varies from p_i at one node to p_j at the other, the node at the heavier end takes more. The shares are those of the bar element, and their total and their moment about either node are the two checks:
EQUATION : [equation v0_lin: source not available in the page]
## Body force: self-weight
A uniform body force is shared by all four nodes, a quarter each, because every N_i integrates to ab/4. Self-weight, f_y = −ρg = −γ (unit weight γ), acts in −y, so it loads only the v-dofs:
EQUATION : [equation r_body: source not available in the page]
## Worked example · the global load vector of the cantilever (Activity 3, text (3.47))
[Figure: The 2 × 2 mesh: node n carries U_{2n−1} (x) and U_{2n} (y).]
Elements 2 (nodes 2, 3, 6, 5) and 4 (nodes 5, 6, 9, 8) have their side 2–3 on the free end. Each puts −2500 N on its local v_2 and v_3, which are global U_6, U_{12} for element 2 and U_{12}, U_{18} for element 4. Node 6 is shared, so U_{12} collects −5000 N: the full 5 kN m^{−1} × 1 m of edge around it.
EQUATION (3.47): [equation r_R: source not available in the page]
The six entries B_i at the fixed dofs 1, 2, 7, 8, 13 and 14 are the unknown support reactions. The total applied load is −10 000 N, which the reactions must balance.
Key points:
- Uniform edge load: p ℓ/2 at each of the two edge nodes, only in the dofs of its direction.
- Linearly varying: ℓ(2p_i + p_j)/6 and ℓ(p_i + 2p_j)/6; self-weight: γtab/4 in each v-dof.
- Cantilever: R_6 = R_{18} = −2500 N, R_{12} = −5000 N; six unknown reactions.
Quick check (not graded): The self-weight of an element a × b of thickness t and unit weight γ is shared as
Options: −γtab/2 at the two bottom nodes | −γtab/4 in each of the four v-dofs | −γtab/8 in all eight dofs
Explanation shown after answering: Each shape function integrates to ab/4, so each node carries a quarter of the weight γtab, and the weight acts in −y: only v_1…v_4 are loaded. Putting it all on the bottom nodes, or into the u-dofs, changes the load the element feels.

[notes-n5] Notes 5. Assembly with two dofs per node, supports and the solution
Assembly is the heat-transfer scatter-add with one extra step: node numbers become dof numbers. Node n owns U_{2n−1} (x) and U_{2n} (y), so each element’s four nodes give eight global dofs, in local order.

## Worked step · entries of the assembled [K] (Activity 4)
Local k_{11} of element 2 (its local node 1 is global node 2) goes to K_{3,3}; local k_{34} = s_6 = −0.373 × 10⁶ goes to K_{5,6}, the u–v coupling of node 3. The diagonals collect s_1 once for every element at the node:
EQUATION : [equation v0_Kdiag: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation v0_K910: source not available in the page]
K_{9,10} is zero: at an interior node of a regular mesh the u–v couplings of the four elements cancel in pairs. K_{3,3} = 1.751 and K_{9,9} = 3.501 (× 10⁶) are visible in the text’s (3.46): a quick check of your dof map.
## Supports: strike the fixed dofs
The three nodes of the left edge are fixed in both directions: six known displacements, all zero. As for a prescribed temperature, their rows and columns are deleted; nothing moves to the right-hand side because the known values are zero. Twelve equations remain, text (3.48), which MATLAB solves.

## Read the solution like a structural engineer (Activity 5)
- The bottom fibre shortens (u_2, u_3 < 0) and the top lengthens (u_8, u_9 > 0) by the same amounts: antisymmetric bending about mid-height, an exact property of this symmetric mesh and load.
- u = 0 at nodes 5 and 6: the mid-height line is the neutral axis.
- v is almost the same across the depth of each section (−0.1306, −0.1304, −0.1306 m at the free end): the depth hardly changes, the usual beam assumption.
## Reactions: the first check of any solution
Evaluate the struck rows, [K]{U} − {R}, at the six fixed dofs. Their sum must balance the applied load and their moment must balance its moment about the fixed edge. The 2 × 2 mesh gives exactly these values, as every correct model must, whatever its mesh:
EQUATION : [equation v0_react: source not available in the page]
Key points:
- Dof map: node n → 2n − 1, 2n; scatter-add 8 × 8 blocks; K_{ii} collects s_1 (or s_9) once per element at the node.
- Six fixed dofs struck → 12 × 12; tip v = −0.1306 m.
- Reactions: ΣR_y = +10 kN, moment 40 kN·m about the fixed edge.
Quick check (not graded): In the 2 × 2 cantilever, why is u = 0 at nodes 5 and 6?
Options: They are fixed by the supports | Their rows were struck from [K] | They lie on the neutral axis of the bending plate
Explanation shown after answering: Under bending the fibres above mid-height stretch and those below shorten by the same amount, so the mid-height line neither stretches nor shortens. Only nodes 1, 4 and 7 are supported, and only their rows were struck.

[notes-n6] Notes 6. Is the answer right? Beam theory, refinement and shear locking
The computer will always return numbers. Whether they are right is the engineer’s question, and it has two independent answers: compare with a simpler theory, and refine the mesh until the answer stops moving.
## A hand check: Timoshenko beam theory
The plate is a deep cantilever (L/H = 2) carrying P = q_yH = 10 kN at its end. Elementary bending gives PL³/(3EI); because the beam is deep, shear deformation adds PL/(κGA) with κ = 5/6:
EQUATION : [equation r_beam: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation r_beam_num: source not available in the page]
EQUATION : [equation v0_err: source not available in the page]
Keep four figures when the difference is small Rounded to three decimals, 0.189 against 0.192, the 16 × 16 error would look like −1.6%; with four figures, as on the Activity 6 slide, it is −1.4%. A percentage difference of two close numbers is only as good as the digits you keep.
[Figure: The hand mesh deflects about two thirds as much as the converged mesh. Each bilinear element keeps straight edges, so it cannot curve; under bending it develops a spurious shear strain and resists with a shear stiffness it should not have. This is shear locking.]

Shape matters more than count Eight elements in three layouts: 4 × 2 gives −0.164 m, 8 × 1 gives −0.166 m, but 2 × 4 gives only −0.133 m. Elements that are long in the bending direction (a/b = 4 in the 2 × 4 mesh) lock most. Refine along the length first. The project rule Three meshes, one table, one independent check (beam theory, the reactions, or a textbook solution). Then, and only then, a conclusion. Never report a single-mesh answer.
## The script, as a diff against Heat Transfer Part 2
% ---- changes from the heat script ----
Lx = 4; Ly = 2; % plate 4 m x 2 m
E = 200e6; nu = 0.33; t = 0.01;
Nx = 2; Ny = 2; ndof = 18; % 2 dofs per node
a = Lx/Nx; b = Ly/Ny;
% 12 closed-form values, text (3.42)
s1 = E*t*((1-nu)*a^2 + 2*b^2)/(6*(1-nu^2)*a*b);
s2 = E*t*((1-nu) + 2*nu)/(8*(1-nu^2));
% ... s3 to s12 likewise ...
k = [s1 s2 s3 s4 s5 s6 s7 s8; ...]; % 8 x 8 pattern of (3.42)
% assembly with the dof map (node n -> 2n-1, 2n)
K = zeros(ndof); F = zeros(ndof,1);
d1 = [1 2 3 4 9 10 7 8]; K(d1,d1) = K(d1,d1) + k;
d2 = [3 4 5 6 11 12 9 10]; K(d2,d2) = K(d2,d2) + k;
d3 = [7 8 9 10 15 16 13 14]; K(d3,d3) = K(d3,d3) + k;
d4 = [9 10 11 12 17 18 15 16]; K(d4,d4) = K(d4,d4) + k;
F([6 12 18]) = [-2500 -5000 -2500]; % edge traction, (3.47)
fixed = [1 2 7 8 13 14]; free = setdiff(1:ndof, fixed);
U = zeros(ndof,1); U(free) = K(free,free) \ F(free); % (3.49)
- Two dofs per node: ndof = 2 × nodes, and each element’s dof list replaces its node list.
- The 4 × 4 conductance pattern becomes the 8 × 8 pattern of (3.42).
- Loads in the v-dofs of the loaded edge; six fixed dofs instead of fixed temperatures. The solve line is unchanged.
The Python version, fe_plane_stress.py, is in the Explorer tab; it builds [k] by Gauss quadrature, reproduces (3.49) and runs the convergence study above.
Key points:
- Two independent checks: beam theory (0.192 m) and mesh refinement; plus the reactions.
- The 2 × 2 Q4 mesh is 32% too stiff: straight-sided elements lock in bending.
- About 32 elements along the length for 1%; elements long in the bending direction lock most.
Quick check (not graded): The same eight Q4 elements as a 4 × 2 mesh or as a 2 × 4 mesh. Which is stiffer?
Options: 2 × 4: its elements are four times longer than deep and lock in bending | 4 × 2: it has more elements along the length | Neither: the same number of elements gives the same stiffness
Explanation shown after answering: 2 × 4 gives −0.133 m against −0.164 m for 4 × 2: the 2 m × 0.5 m elements cannot curve along their length, so they develop most spurious shear. The count of elements is the same; their shape is not.

[glossary-galerkin-vector-version] Glossary: Galerkin, vector version
Galerkin, vector version: Weighted residual with [N]ᵀ as the weight: eight equations per four-node element, one per dof.

[glossary-strain-displacement-matrix-b] Glossary: strain–displacement matrix [B]
strain–displacement matrix [B]: [B] = [∂]ᵀ[N], 3 × 8: the strains {ε} = [B]{û} at any point of the element; each row sums to zero.

[glossary-stiffness-matrix-k] Glossary: stiffness matrix [k]
stiffness matrix [k]: t∫[B]ᵀ[E][B] dA, 8 × 8, symmetric; units force per length (N m^{−1} or kN m^{−1} ).

[glossary-stiffness-influence-coefficient-k-ij] Glossary: stiffness influence coefficient k_{ij}
stiffness influence coefficient k_{ij}: Force at dof i needed to give dof j a unit displacement with every other dof held.

[glossary-s-1-s-12] Glossary: s_1 …s_{12}
s_1 …s_{12}: The twelve distinct entries of a rectangle’s [k], text (3.42); s_2 , s_4 , s_6 , s_8 (u–v couplings) do not depend on a, b.

[glossary-e-1] Glossary: Ē = E/(1 − ν²)
Ē = E/(1 − ν²): The plane-stress modulus that multiplies the normal terms of [E]; G = Ē(1 − ν)/2 is the shear modulus.

[glossary-zero-energy-rigid-body-modes] Glossary: zero-energy (rigid-body) modes
zero-energy (rigid-body) modes: Two translations and one rotation that cause no strain; [k]{d} = 0 for each, so [k] is singular until supported.

[glossary-row-sum-check] Glossary: row-sum check
row-sum check: In every row of [k] the u-entries and the v-entries each add up to zero.

[glossary-gauss-quadrature] Glossary: Gauss quadrature
Gauss quadrature: Numerical integration at chosen points; 2 × 2 points integrate the Q4 [k] of a rectangle exactly.

[glossary-consistent-equivalent-nodal-loads] Glossary: consistent (equivalent) nodal loads
consistent (equivalent) nodal loads: Nodal forces that do the same work as a distributed load; a uniform edge load gives pℓ/2 to each edge node.

[glossary-traction-line-load] Glossary: traction · line load
traction · line load: Traction is force per unit area of edge (kN m^{−2} ); a line load is per unit length for the whole thickness (kN m^{−1} ) = traction × t.

[glossary-body-force-self-weight] Glossary: body force · self-weight
body force · self-weight: Force per unit volume; self-weight γ gives −γtab/4 in each v-dof of a Q4 element.

[glossary-dof-map] Glossary: dof map
dof map: Node n → dofs 2n − 1 (u) and 2n (v); an element’s eight global dofs in local order.

[glossary-scatter-add] Glossary: scatter-add
scatter-add: K_{IJ} += k_{ij} with I, J from the dof map; the same for {R}.

[glossary-bandwidth] Glossary: bandwidth
bandwidth: How far the non-zeros of [K] spread from the diagonal; nodes numbered close together keep it narrow.

[glossary-fixed-dofs-reduced-system] Glossary: fixed dofs · reduced system
fixed dofs · reduced system: Known displacements struck by row–column elimination; 18 − 6 = 12 equations for the 2 × 2 cantilever.

[glossary-reactions] Glossary: reactions
reactions: The struck rows [K]{U} − {R} at the supports; they must balance the applied loads and their moment.

[glossary-neutral-axis] Glossary: neutral axis
neutral axis: The line that neither stretches nor shortens in bending; mid-height of the cantilever (u = 0 at nodes 5 and 6).

[glossary-timoshenko-beam] Glossary: Timoshenko beam
Timoshenko beam: Beam theory with shear deformation: δ = PL³/(3EI) + PL/(κGA), κ = 5/6 for a rectangle; 0.192 m for the text’s cantilever.

[glossary-shear-locking] Glossary: shear locking
shear locking: Bilinear elements with straight edges cannot curve, develop spurious shear in bending and are too stiff; worst when long in the bending direction.

[glossary-convergence-study] Glossary: convergence study
convergence study: The same model on at least three meshes, tabulated, until the result stops changing.

[glossary-patch-test] Glossary: patch test
patch test: An element must reproduce a uniform state of stress exactly; one Q4 in uniform tension on rollers does.
